FOR HOME SELLERS AND LISTING AGENTS

See cash at closing — and whether the higher offer actually pays more.

After NAR, buyer-broker compensation is a negotiated line, not an automatic split of “the commission.” Enter the offer, the payoff, and the costs. The worksheet shows net to the seller, the sale price that hits a target net, and a side-by-side of two offers. Everything runs in this page; nothing is uploaded.

The share link carries every number on this page in the part of the URL after the #, which browsers never send to a server. Anyone you send it to opens this worksheet already filled in — and can change the payoff or a rate to see their own figure.

Transparent arithmetic from your inputs — not a closing disclosure, a tax opinion, or advice about which offer to accept. Confirm every line with title/escrow, the lender payoff, and your broker.

What this checks

Generic “seller closing cost” pages still treat commission as one percentage. The decision sellers actually face after NAR is which offer leaves more cash once buyer-broker compensation and concessions are separate lines. Higher offer vs cleaner offer walks through that in search-query words, and this calculator vs. your title company's net sheet explains which of the two to reach for at which point in the sale, and this calculator vs. Zillow's Home Sale Calculator covers the earlier, rougher estimate most sellers see first, and this calculator vs. HomeLight's Net Proceeds Calculator covers the estimate that leads toward an agent referral.

It does not recommend a list price, a commission, or an offer, and it is not legal, tax, or real-estate advice. The gap between offers is an arithmetic comparison of the rates you entered.

Common questions

How do I calculate how much I will net from selling my house?

Start with the offer price. Subtract the loan payoff, the listing broker fee, any buyer-broker compensation the seller agrees to pay, other concessions, title and escrow, transfer tax, prorations, and remaining closing costs. What remains is an estimate of cash to the seller. This page does that arithmetic from the numbers you enter; it is not a closing disclosure.

Is the higher offer always more money for the seller after NAR?

No. Buyer-broker compensation is now a negotiated amount, not an automatic split of a 5% or 6% commission. A higher offer that asks the seller to pay the buyer’s broker and closing costs can leave less cash than a cleaner, lower offer. Compare both on a net sheet before deciding.

What sale price do I need to walk away with a target amount?

Enter the net you want, the loan payoff, and the same cost rates. Percentage fees scale with price; flat fees and the payoff do not. The calculator solves for the sale price that produces that net on those assumptions. Confirm the figure with title or escrow before listing or countering.

How do I estimate the Tax / HOA proration figure above?

Take the annual property tax bill and divide by 365 for a daily rate, then multiply by the number of days in the tax period the seller is responsible for through closing. A $3,650 annual bill is $10/day; 80 days charged to the seller comes to $800 — which is why that field defaults to $800 above. The Estimate it box under the field does this arithmetic for you: enter the annual tax and the days charged, then Use this estimate fills the proration field for you. Whether the seller owes days before or after closing depends on whether your local jurisdiction bills taxes in advance or in arrears, so use the title company's proration once you have it; this is a starting estimate, not the number on the closing statement.

offer-comparison.html.text:
SELLER NET SHEET

The higher offer is not always more cash.

A listing agent used to say “we’ll look at the net.” After NAR that sentence actually means something. Buyer-broker compensation is no longer an automatic split of a 5% or 6% commission. It is a number on the offer — or it is absent.

Take two offers on the same house. Offer A is $425,000 and asks the seller to pay 2.5% to the buyer’s broker plus $8,000 toward the buyer’s closing costs. Offer B is $417,000 with neither. The loan payoff and the title bill are the same. On those assumptions, Offer B can leave the seller more money. The extra price on A does not cover the extra concessions.

That is not a recommendation to take the lower offer. Inspection, earnest money, financing, and timing still matter, and local transfer tax and proration customs change the dollars. It is a reason to put both offers on the same worksheet before anyone says “the higher one wins.”

  • Keep listing-broker pay and buyer-broker pay on separate lines.
  • Put seller-paid closing help on its own line, not inside “commission.”
  • Solve backward from the cash the seller needs, then see which offer clears it.

Open the seller net sheet calculator and compare the two offers on this page’s numbers — then replace every rate with the title company’s estimate.

Common questions

Can a lower offer net a home seller more money?

Yes, if the higher offer asks the seller to pay the buyer’s broker and closing costs. Those lines come out of the seller’s proceeds. A cleaner offer at a lower price can leave more cash after the payoff. Compare both on a seller net sheet before deciding.

Do sellers still automatically pay the buyer’s agent after NAR?

No. Buyer-broker compensation is negotiated. A seller may offer it, a buyer may pay their own broker, or the amount may be zero. Treat it as its own line on the net sheet rather than half of a 5% or 6% commission.

No warranty. This page is provided free and as-is. It is not legal, tax, financial, or real-estate advice. Confirm figures with title/escrow, the lender, and your broker before accepting or countering an offer.

This calculator vs. HomeLight's Net Proceeds Calculator

HomeLight's Net Proceeds Calculator is a free estimator, published as part of an agent-matching business, that starts from an estimated home value to give a rough sense of proceeds before you have an offer. This page starts from an offer you actually have and compares two offers side by side — with nothing sent to a server and no expert-matching flow.

What each one is for

HomeLight's Net Proceeds Calculator is a free estimator on HomeLight's own site. Per HomeLight's own description, it takes an estimated home value, a remaining mortgage balance, real estate agent commissions, and seller preparation and closing costs, and produces what HomeLight itself calls a rough estimate based on a traditional, agent-assisted home sale. HomeLight separately publishes a Cash Offer Comparison Tool that, per its own description, compares a cash offer side by side with an agent-led sale estimate — a comparison between two different sale paths, not between two real offers of the same kind.

This page starts one step later: after a listing agreement exists and an offer is on the table. It takes the actual sale price on that offer (or two competing offers) and the actual rates from your listing agreement and closing estimate — not an estimated home value — and turns them into cash to the seller.

HomeLight is a real estate agent-matching company, and its own net-proceeds content directs a seller toward "Talk to an Expert" for a full cost and proceeds breakdown — a reasonable next step for a business built on referring sellers to agents, and worth knowing plainly rather than discovering partway through. This page has no expert-matching flow, no lead form, and no account: it is arithmetic that runs on your own device and stops there.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What might my house net, roughly, before I have listed it or received an offer?HomeLight's Net Proceeds Calculator — it is built to estimate from an estimated home value.
What does this specific offer actually net, using my real listing-agreement rate and closing estimate?This calculator — every figure is one you enter from your own paperwork, not an estimated value.
Which of two offers in front of me right now leaves more cash?This calculator's offer comparison — both offers side by side on the same assumptions.
How does a cash offer compare to an agent-led sale, in general?HomeLight's Cash Offer Comparison Tool — built for that specific question, which this calculator does not answer.
Do I need an account, or does using it lead toward an agent referral?This calculator: no account, no lead form, nothing sent anywhere. HomeLight's tool runs inside an agent-matching business.

The two answer different moments rather than competing for the same one: HomeLight's calculator for a rough estimate before a listing or an offer exists, this page for the decision between real offers once they do. This calculator is arithmetic, not a closing disclosure or a valuation, and it is not a substitute for a title company, escrow officer, attorney, or tax adviser.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Different starting points. HomeLight's Net Proceeds Calculator, per HomeLight's own description of it, takes an estimated home value, a remaining mortgage balance, real estate agent commissions, and seller preparation and closing costs, and produces what HomeLight itself calls a rough estimate based on a traditional, agent-assisted home sale — useful before you have listed or received an offer. This page starts from a real number: the price on an offer you actually received (or two, side by side), and turns it into cash at closing using the rates from your own listing agreement and closing estimate rather than an estimated value. Use HomeLight's tool for an early, rough estimate; use this one once offers exist and you are deciding between them.

Does HomeLight's calculator compare two competing offers side by side?

Not the same comparison. HomeLight publishes a separate Cash Offer Comparison Tool that, per HomeLight's own description, compares a cash offer side by side with an agent-led sale estimate — one sale path against another, not two real offers of the same kind that a seller has actually received. This page's offer comparison holds the loan payoff and closing-cost assumptions constant and puts two full offers next to each other, so the number that changes is the one that actually differs between them.

Where does HomeLight's calculator send me next?

HomeLight is a real estate agent-matching company, and its own net-proceeds content directs sellers to "Talk to an Expert" for a full cost and proceeds breakdown — consistent with a business built on referring sellers to agents. That is a reasonable thing for HomeLight to offer and not a criticism of it. This page has no expert-matching flow of any kind: it is a static calculator with no lead capture.

No. This calculator runs entirely on your own device: there is no account, no address lookup, and nothing you enter is sent anywhere. HomeLight's calculator runs on HomeLight's own site as part of a real estate agent-matching business, which is reasonable for what it is and worth knowing if you would rather not have a proceeds estimate tied to an agent-referral flow.

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by HomeLight. HomeLight is a trademark of HomeLight, Inc., named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not, based on HomeLight's own public description of its Net Proceeds Calculator and Cash Offer Comparison Tool.

vs-title-company-net-sheet.html.text:
← Seller Net Sheet Calculator

This calculator vs. your title company's net sheet

Two different moments in the same sale. A title or escrow company's estimated net sheet settles one accepted contract with the real, local, quoted figures. This page is a free, private worksheet for the hours before that — when two offers are on the table and you have to pick one.

What each one is for

Your title or escrow company's estimated seller net sheet is the authoritative document, and you should ask for one. It is prepared for your transaction using figures nobody else has: the company's own title and escrow charges, the recording fees and transfer taxes that apply in the county where the property actually sits, your lender's payoff, and prorations calculated to your specific closing date. Where its numbers and this page's numbers disagree, the title company's are the ones that govern.

What it is not is instant. It is normally prepared on request and around a particular contract, which makes it an awkward instrument for the decision that comes first — when two offers are sitting in front of you and the response deadline is measured in hours. This calculator fills that gap: the same arithmetic, in your browser, immediately, re-runnable as many times as you want, with no account and nothing uploaded. Enter the rates from a title or escrow estimate rather than guessing them and the two agree.

It also runs the arithmetic in two directions a prepared net sheet does not. It compares two offers on the same house side by side, holding payoff, title, transfer tax, and proration assumptions constant so only the terms that genuinely differ move the result. And it solves backwards for the sale price that produces a target net — the question a seller asks when they already know what they need to walk away with.

One modelling difference is worth stating plainly, because it is the reason this tool disagrees with most “seller closing cost calculator” pages. After the NAR settlement, commission is not one blended percentage. Listing-broker pay is a contract between the seller and their own broker. Buyer-broker compensation is separately a negotiated seller concession, a buyer-paid amount, or nothing. Collapsing the two into a single rate hides precisely the variable that differs between competing offers — and therefore the variable that decides which offer nets more.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What will I actually net on the contract I have accepted, using my county's real fees and my closing date?Your title or escrow company's estimated net sheet — the authoritative figure, and this calculator does not replace it.
Which of these two offers leaves me more cash, right now, before the deadline?This calculator's offer comparison — free, instant, private, no account.
What does the house have to sell for if I need to walk away with a particular number?This calculator's target-net solver, which inverts the same arithmetic.
Does a higher headline price always mean more money?This calculator — it separates buyer-broker compensation and concessions, which is where a bigger offer quietly becomes a smaller one.
What are the actual title, escrow, recording, and transfer-tax rates for my property?Your title or escrow company. Type their figures into this calculator rather than estimating them.
How do the two offers compare line by line, on one page?This calculator's offer comparison.
Do I need an account or a sign-in?This calculator: no. A title company net sheet is requested from the company handling your closing.

The two are sequential rather than competing: this page for the decision between offers, a title or escrow company's estimate for the contract you accept. This calculator is arithmetic, not a closing disclosure, and it is not a substitute for a title company, escrow officer, attorney, or tax adviser.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or ask my title company for a net sheet?

Both, at different moments, and the title company's version is the authoritative one. A title or escrow company prepares an estimated seller net sheet using the actual fees for your county and your transaction: their own title and escrow charges, the recording and transfer taxes that apply where the property sits, and the payoff and proration figures for your specific closing date. Ask for it, and treat it as the number that governs. What it is not is instant, and it is normally prepared around a particular contract — which makes it an awkward fit for the question that comes first, when two offers are sitting on the table and you have hours rather than days to decide. That is the gap this calculator fills: it runs the same arithmetic in your browser, immediately, as many times as you like, so you can see which offer leaves more cash before you accept one. Enter the rates from your title or escrow estimate rather than guessing them, and the two agree; where they differ, the title company is right.

Why does this calculator split listing-broker pay from buyer-broker compensation?

Because after the NAR settlement they are genuinely two different things, and most seller closing-cost calculators still model commission as one blended percentage. Listing-broker pay is a contract between the seller and their own broker. Buyer-broker compensation is separately a negotiated seller concession, a buyer-paid amount, or nothing at all — it is not automatically half of five or six percent. Collapsing the two into a single rate hides exactly the variable that differs between competing offers, which is the variable that decides which offer nets more.

Can a higher offer really net less than a lower one?

Yes, and it is the ordinary case rather than a curiosity. Buyer-broker compensation and seller concessions such as closing-cost help or repair credits come out of the same proceeds as everything else, so an offer with a larger headline price that asks for more of both can leave less cash at closing than a cleaner, lower one. This calculator's worked example is a 425,000 offer asking 2.5 percent buyer-broker pay plus 8,000 in closing help, which nets below a cleaner 417,000 offer. Comparing headline prices is what this tool exists to stop.

What does this calculator do that a net sheet does not?

Two things, both of which run the arithmetic in a direction a prepared net sheet does not. It compares two offers on the same house side by side, holding the payoff, title, transfer tax, and proration assumptions constant so that only the terms that actually differ move the result. And it solves backwards for the sale price that produces a target net — the question a seller asks when they know what they need to walk away with and want to know what the house has to sell for to get there.

Does anything I type here leave my browser?

No. The arithmetic runs on your own device, there is no account to create, and no payoff amount, address, price, or rate is uploaded anywhere. Once the page has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Open the Seller Net Sheet Calculator to run your own numbers.

Verify every figure against your own title or escrow estimate before relying on it.

This calculator vs. Zillow's Home Sale Calculator

Zillow's Home Sale Calculator is a free, well-known estimator that starts from a Zestimate and one blended commission line, to give a rough sense of proceeds before you have an offer. This page starts from an offer you actually have, splits buyer-broker compensation out as its own negotiated line, and compares two offers side by side — with nothing sent to a server.

What each one is for

Zillow's Home Sale Calculator is a free estimator on Zillow's own site. Per Zillow's own description, it begins from your home's Zestimate — Zillow's automated valuation estimate — or a price you enter, then walks through typical selling costs (agent commission, closing costs, mortgage payoff, home-prep and repair costs) to estimate what a sale would net. It is a reasonable place to start before you have listed a house or received an offer, and it lives inside Zillow's real estate marketplace, where a saved estimate can be tied to a Zillow account and a Zestimate for the property.

This page starts one step later: after a listing agreement exists and an offer is on the table. It takes the actual sale price on that offer (or two competing offers) and the actual rates from your listing agreement and closing estimate — not a typical range — and turns them into cash to the seller.

One modelling difference is worth stating plainly, because it is the reason this tool's number can disagree with a blended-commission estimate. Zillow's own published guidance describes agent commission as sellers typically paying both their own agent and the buyer's agent, each around 2-3% of the sale price — a combined commission figure. After the NAR settlement, buyer-broker compensation is a separately negotiated seller concession, not an automatic split of one blended rate, and it can differ between two offers on the same house. This page keeps listing-broker pay and buyer-broker compensation on two independent lines for exactly that reason.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Zillow's Home Sale Calculator?

Different starting points, and both are useful. Zillow's Home Sale Calculator is a free tool on Zillow's own site that begins from a Zestimate — Zillow's automated estimate of what a home is worth — and walks through typical selling costs to estimate proceeds before you have an offer in hand. Zillow's own published guidance on the calculator describes agent commission as a combined figure — sellers typically paying both their listing agent and the buyer's agent, at roughly 2-3% of the sale price each — presented as one commission line rather than as a separately negotiated seller concession. This page treats listing-broker pay and buyer-broker compensation as two distinct, independently entered lines on purpose: after the NAR settlement, buyer-broker compensation is a negotiated amount that can differ between two offers on the same house, and a single blended commission rate cannot show that difference. That difference is exactly what decides which of two offers actually nets more.
